canonical_statement: The study aimed to examine bleeding rates in hospitalized patients with AF/AFL treated with intravenous UFH and to propose a dosing strategy intended to minimize bleeding risk.
The study used a retrospective medical-record review at New York University Langone Medical Center and Bellevue Hospital Center.

Eligible patients were adults at least 18 years old with newly or previously diagnosed AF/AFL who received UFH for more than 24 hours specifically for non-valvular AF/AFL between December 2009 and January 2011.

population.label: Eligible hospitalized adults
inclusion_criteria: UFH >24 hours specifically for non-valvular AF/AFL

canonical_statement: Patients were excluded for a recent alternative indication for anticoagulation, including mechanical heart valve, pulmonary embolism, deep venous thrombosis, acute coronary syndrome, or left ventricular thrombus within the preceding 7 days.

population.label: Screened AF/AFL patients
exclusion_criteria: Alternative anticoagulation indication within 7 days: mechanical heart valve, PE, DVT, ACS, or left ventricular thrombus

canonical_statement: Patients were also excluded for stroke or transient ischemic attack within 30 days, prior intracranial hemorrhage, sepsis, or postoperative states that could alter coagulation.
Collected data included baseline demographics, serial aPTT measurements, UFH bolus doses and initial infusion rates, hemoglobin values, bleeding events, stroke, and thromboembolic phenomena.
Study data were collected and managed with REDCap electronic data-capture tools.

Major bleeding used International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis criteria: fatal bleeding; symptomatic bleeding in a critical area or organ; hemoglobin decrease >2 g/dL; or bleeding requiring at least two units of whole blood or packed red blood cells.

outcome.definition: Major bleeding used International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis criteria: fatal bleeding; symptomatic bleeding in a critical area or organ; hemoglobin decrease >2 g/dL; or bleeding requiring at least two units of whole blood or packed red blood cells.

canonical_statement: Clinically relevant non-major bleeding was defined as overt bleeding documented by a physician or nurse that was not attributable to an alternative source.

outcome.definition: Clinically relevant non-major bleeding was defined as overt bleeding documented by a physician or nurse that was not attributable to an alternative source.

canonical_statement: Therapeutic anticoagulation was defined as an aPTT of 49-65 seconds, corresponding to 1.5-2.0 times the mean of the normal aPTT range.

outcome.definition: aPTT 49-65 seconds (1.5-2.0 times mean normal aPTT)

canonical_statement: Continuous-variable distributions were assessed with quantile-quantile plots, histograms, and the Shapiro-Wilks test of normality.
Because continuous variables deviated significantly from normality, the Wilcoxon Signed Ranked Test was used for between-group bleeding comparisons.

Initial weight-based UFH infusion rates were regressed against resultant aPTT values; the authors repeated the regression on a transformed scale to assess heteroscedasticity and reported that the relationship persisted.

After identifying an infusion-rate threshold associated with bleeding in univariate analysis, the multivariable bleeding model assessed age, hypertension, renal insufficiency, prior bleeding, prior stroke, aspirin use, and thienopyridine use as potential confounders.
A total of 996 hospitalized patients with AF/AFL who received UFH met the initial screening criteria.
94 patients were excluded for acute coronary syndrome within the preceding 7 days.
50 patients were excluded for active bleeding or cardiac thrombosis at anticoagulation initiation.
115 patients were excluded because of incomplete data or misdiagnosis.
129 patients were excluded for a history of coagulopathy, recent CVA within 30 days, PE/DVT, or intracerebral hemorrhage.
243 patients were excluded for a postoperative state within the preceding 7 days.
47 patients were excluded for sepsis.
4 patients were excluded for being out of the age criteria.
88 patients were excluded for mechanical heart valves.
After exclusions, 226 patients were included in the primary analysis.
The mean age of the analysis cohort was 71.2 +/- 1.8 years.
Male patients comprised 52.0% of the analysis cohort.
White patients comprised 71.7% of the analysis cohort.
Black patients comprised 8.9% of the analysis cohort.
Hispanic patients comprised 12.0% of the analysis cohort.
Asian patients comprised 6.2% of the analysis cohort.
Patients of other race/ethnicity comprised 1.3% of the analysis cohort.
Mean BMI was 28.5 +/- 1.0 kg/m2.
Current smokers comprised 8.4% of the cohort.
Former smokers comprised 40.7% of the cohort.
Never smokers comprised 50.4% of the cohort.
Hypertension was present in 74.3% of the cohort.
Hyperlipidemia was present in 52.2% of the cohort.
Diabetes mellitus was present in 32.7% of the cohort.
Coronary artery disease was present in 40.7% of the cohort.
Congestive heart failure was present in 34.5% of the cohort.
Prior CVA/TIA was present in 14.6% of the cohort.
Renal insufficiency was present in 19.0% of the cohort.
Peripheral arterial disease was present in 12.8% of the cohort.
A prior history of bleeding was present in 4.9% of the cohort.
Mean CHADS2 score was 2.1 +/- 0.2.
A CHADS2 score >=3 was present in 34.1% of the cohort.
Mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 3.6 +/- 0.2.
A CHA2DS2-VASc score >=5 was present in 32.7% of the cohort.
Aspirin was an outpatient medication in 43.8% of the cohort.
Clopidogrel was an outpatient medication in 6.6% of the cohort.
Beta-blockers were outpatient medications in 60.0% of the cohort.
Calcium-channel blockers were outpatient medications in 35.0% of the cohort.
Digoxin was an outpatient medication in 26.5% of the cohort.
Warfarin was an outpatient medication in 56.6% of the cohort.
Baseline aPTT was 31.6 +/- 0.6 seconds.
Baseline hemoglobin was 12.7 +/- 0.3 g/dL.
Baseline platelet count was 245 +/- 12 x10^3/microL.
Baseline creatinine was 1.3 +/- 0.1 mg/dL.
Ninety-eight patients (43%) received an initial UFH bolus.
Among patients who received an initial UFH bolus, the median bolus dose was 49.4 U/kg (IQR 39.8-61.4 U/kg).

population.label: Patients receiving an initial UFH bolus

canonical_statement: The first aPTT was checked a median of 6.7 hours after UFH initiation (IQR 5.9-8.0 hours).
At the first aPTT check, 56.1% of patients given an initial UFH bolus versus 56.3% without a bolus had exceeded the therapeutic threshold of 49 seconds; p=0.99.
Bleeding occurred in 35.7% of patients who received an initial UFH bolus and 31.3% of those who did not; p=0.48.
Under the non-standardized UFH dosing used in the cohort, 21% of patients remained in the therapeutic aPTT range throughout the study.
Under the non-standardized UFH dosing used in the cohort, 51% of patients were above the therapeutic aPTT range.

concept.text: aPTT above therapeutic range during UFH therapy

canonical_statement: Linear regression related aPTT to initial UFH infusion rate as aPTT = 7.8 x (initial infusion rate) - 26.08, with R=0.74.
Using the best-fit regression curve, the authors reported that initial UFH infusion rates of 9.7-11.8 U/kg/h could attain therapeutic anticoagulation levels.
Bleeding events occurred in 76 of 226 patients (34%).
Bleeding events occurred an average of 1.4 days after UFH initiation.

concept.text: Time from UFH initiation to bleeding

canonical_statement: Twenty-five percent of bleeding events met the study definition of major bleeding.
Patients without bleeding had a median initial UFH infusion rate of 11.4 U/kg/h (IQR 9.2-14.2).
Patients with any bleeding had a median initial UFH infusion rate of 13.3 U/kg/h (IQR 10.5-14.3), significantly higher than patients without bleeding; p=0.012.
Patients with major bleeding had a median initial UFH infusion rate of 14.2 U/kg/h (IQR 11.1-15.5), significantly higher than patients without bleeding; p=0.016.
Patients with clinically relevant non-major bleeding had a median initial UFH infusion rate of 13.2 U/kg/h (IQR 10.3-14.2), significantly higher than patients without bleeding; p=0.049.

population.label: Patients with clinically relevant non-major bleeding

canonical_statement: In univariate analysis, an initial UFH infusion rate above 11.0 U/kg/h was associated with any bleeding with OR 1.82 (95% CI 1.02-3.24), p=0.04.
Sixty-one percent of patients received initial UFH infusion rates above 11.0 U/kg/h.
The reported number needed to cause one bleeding event with an initial UFH infusion rate above 11.0 U/kg/h was 7.07.
In the multivariable bleeding model, Initial UFH infusion rate >11 U/kg/h had an adjusted OR 1.95 (95% CI 1.06-3.59), p=0.03 for bleeding.
In the multivariable bleeding model, Age >65 years had an adjusted OR 1.06 (95% CI 0.52-2.17), p=0.87 for bleeding.
In the multivariable bleeding model, Creatinine >2.6 g/dL had an adjusted OR 0.15 (95% CI 0.02-1.17), p=0.07 for bleeding.
In the multivariable bleeding model, History of hypertension had an adjusted OR 1.42 (95% CI 0.7-2.88), p=0.34 for bleeding.
In the multivariable bleeding model, History of prior stroke had an adjusted OR 0.83 (95% CI 0.34-2.03), p=0.69 for bleeding.
In the multivariable bleeding model, History of prior bleeding event had an adjusted OR 1.48 (95% CI 0.38-5.77), p=0.57 for bleeding.

concept.text: No history of prior bleeding event

canonical_statement: In the multivariable bleeding model, History of aspirin use had an adjusted OR 1.67 (95% CI 0.93-2.99), p=0.09 for bleeding.
In the multivariable bleeding model, History of thienopyridine use had an adjusted OR 0.58 (95% CI 0.19-1.79), p=0.35 for bleeding.
No strokes were observed during the inpatient hospitalization periods.
No thromboembolic complications were observed during the inpatient hospitalization periods.
The authors concluded that higher initial UFH infusion rates in hospitalized patients with AF/AFL were associated with increased bleeding risk.

The authors proposed an initial UFH infusion rate of 9.7-11.0 U/kg/h without a bolus as a strategy to achieve therapeutic anticoagulation while lowering overall bleeding risk in hospitalized AF/AFL patients.
The authors stated that UFH boluses neither increased bleeding rates nor decreased time to therapeutic aPTT and questioned their clinical utility in AF/AFL.
The analysis was retrospective and therefore subject to hidden biases.
The study was not powered for subgroup analyses by age or gender.
The authors noted that the high bleeding rate could have been partly related to concomitant warfarin and intravenous UFH bridging.
The cohort was drawn from the northeastern United States and was mostly Caucasian, limiting generalizability to the broader US population.
The article disclosed no conflicts: "Disclosures None."
